content.intro: Learn casting and type safety in expressions through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Casting and Type Safety in Expressions matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of casting and type safety in expressions is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Explicit casting in calculations, Resolving incompatible types, Preventing unintended truncation, Safe handling of optional values. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Explicit casting in calculations
items.text: Explicit casting in calculations works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Resolving incompatible types
items.text: Resolving incompatible types helps you transform values with scalar functions and expressions while preserving type safety, numeric precision, time-zone meaning, and NULL semantics. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Type inference in complex expressions
items.text: Type inference in complex expressions works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

content_blocks.code: SELECT CAST(price AS numeric(12,2)) AS exact_price, CAST(stock_quantity AS integer) AS unit_count FROM products ORDER BY product_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: Explicit casts make the intended result types visible. Check rounding and range behavior before narrowing a type.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
